settings.link_label: Crate training with yak chews: the full guide

settings.key_insight: A yak chew isn't just something to keep your dog busy. Used consistently, it becomes a ritual — a signal that tells your dog: this is calm time. That signal is worth more than the chew itself.
settings.article_body:
I didn't set out to build a calm-time product. I set out to build a better chew. But the feedback we kept getting from customers changed how I think about what we make.

"My dog used to bark for 20 minutes when I left. Now I give him a yak chew and he just... settles."

"She used to be anxious during thunderstorms. The chew gives her something to focus on."

"My vet told me to find something to help with his separation anxiety. This is the only thing that's worked."

Why chewing reduces anxiety

Chewing triggers the release of endorphins in dogs. It's a self-soothing behavior — the same reason anxious dogs chew furniture, shoes, and anything else they can find. Giving them an appropriate outlet doesn't just protect your belongings. It actively reduces their stress response.

The key is consistency. A chew given randomly doesn't build a ritual. A chew given at the same time, in the same place, during the same situations — that becomes a signal. Your dog learns: this thing means calm time is starting.

Building the routine

Here's the protocol I recommend:

  1. Pick a trigger. Crate time, alone time, thunderstorms, guests arriving — whatever your dog struggles with.
  2. Give the chew before the trigger hits. Don't wait until your dog is already anxious. Give the chew 2–3 minutes before you leave, before the storm starts, before guests walk in.
  3. Be consistent for 2 weeks. The ritual only works if it's predictable. Same chew, same timing, same location.
  4. Pair with a calm cue. A simple word like "settle" or "easy" said in a low voice as you hand over the chew helps reinforce the association.

What size for calm-time sessions

For calm-time use, I actually recommend sizing down slightly from what you'd give for a full enrichment session. You want the chew to last the duration of the stressful event — not be finished in 10 minutes. A Medium for a 50lb dog, rather than a Large, gives you a longer session.
